procedural_history.originating_court: Court of the Special Judge, Greater Bombay, appointed under the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1952.
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the Special Judge tendering a conditional pardon to a co-accused (Jagasia) and ordering that he be examined as an approver and witness for the prosecution.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant (Fernandes) filed a criminal revision application in the Bombay High Court challenging the Special Judge's order. The prosecution stated it had no objection to the grant of pardon. The High Court dismissed the revision application and upheld the tender of conditional pardon.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant (Fernandes) appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave against the High Court's order. The appellant contended that the Special Judge's powers to tender pardon were limited to applications by the prosecution, that the powers were circumscribed by considerations underlying s. 540 Cr. P. C., and that the Special Judge had not exercised his discretion judicially.

issue.issue_text: Whether the powers of the Special Judge in tendering pardon under s. 8(2) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act are limited to an application by the prosecution, or if the Judge can act suo motu.

facts: A clerk, who was a co-accused in a corruption case, applied to the Special Judge to be made an approver (a witness for the prosecution).
The other co-accused, including the appellant, opposed this application.
The Special Judge, acting under s. 8(2) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, tendered a pardon to the clerk.
The appellant argued that the Special Judge could not do this without an application from the prosecution, i.e., the judge could not act 'suo motu' (on his own initiative).
law: The issue revolves around the interpretation of a Special Judge's power to tender a pardon under s. 8(2) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act.
The appellant's argument was based on a comparison of s. 8(2) with ss. 337 and 338 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.), which also deal with tendering pardons.
Section 8(2) states that a pardon tendered by a Special Judge is 'deemed' to be a pardon under s. 338 Cr.P.C. for the purposes of applying ss. 339 and 339A.
application: The appellant contended that the differences between the powers of a Special Judge under the Act and the powers of other courts under the Cr.P.C. showed that the Special Judge's power was limited and could only be exercised if the prosecution moved an application first.

The Court examined the differences between the sections. It noted that the 'deeming' provision in s. 8(2) was limited in scope; it only meant that the consequences of a pardon (as laid out in ss. 339 and 339A of the Cr.P.C.) would apply. It did not mean the entire procedure of s. 338 was applicable.

The Court acknowledged other differences, such as the fact that a Special Judge cannot order a committing magistrate to tender a pardon because there is no commitment proceeding in a trial before a Special Judge.

However, the Court reasoned that these procedural differences do not lead to the conclusion that the Special Judge's fundamental power to tender a pardon is restricted. The text states that these differences "do not, howe'1er, show that the powers of the [Special Judge are limited]".
By rejecting the appellant's reasoning, the Court implicitly affirmed that the power is not limited to an application by the prosecution.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's contention. It held that the procedural differences between s. 8(2) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act and ss. 337/338 of the Cr.P.C. do not mean that the Special Judge's power to tender a pardon is limited to an application by the prosecution. Therefore, the Judge can act suo motu.

issue.issue_text: Whether the powers of the Special Judge under s. 8(2) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act are circumscribed by the considerations that underlie s. 540 Cr. P. C., such that he could not acquit one accused so as to be able to convict another.

law.law_text: Section 540 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.) confers power on a court to summon material witnesses at any stage of an inquiry, trial, or other proceeding.
Section 8(2) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act gives a Special Judge the power to tender a pardon to an accused person.

application.application_text: The Supreme Court found no merit in the argument that the powers under s. 8(2) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act are governed by s. 540 of the Cr.P.C.
The Court distinguished between the two powers, stating that the power to summon a witness under s. 540 should not be confused with the power to tender a pardon to an accused under s. 8(2).

It reasoned that the considerations for summoning a witness are different from the considerations for tendering a pardon. While both actions must be in the interests of justice, the Court stated that this is where the commonality ends and other distinct considerations arise for each power.

reasoning.conclusion: The Court concluded that it is not possible to read s. 540 of the Cr.P.C. as a limitation on the Special Judge's power to tender a pardon under s. 8(2) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act. Therefore, the Court rejected the argument that the judge's power was circumscribed in such a way that he could not acquit one accused to convict another.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Special Judge had exercised his discretion judicially and properly in tendering the pardon.

facts: An accused clerk in a corruption trial applied directly to the Special Judge to be granted a pardon and become a prosecution witness (an approver).
The Special Judge, acting on his own initiative ('suo motu'), granted the conditional pardon without first consulting the prosecution.
The case was appealed to the High Court, where the Public Prosecutor stated that the prosecution welcomed and favourably considered the tender of pardon to the clerk.
law: Before tendering a pardon, a judge must know the nature of the evidence the person is likely to give and their degree of culpability compared to the other co-accused.
Ordinarily, it is for the prosecution to request that an accused be tendered a pardon.

If an accused applies directly to the judge, the proper course is for the judge to first refer the request to the prosecution for its opinion. The judge should not take it upon themselves to decide the matter without the prosecution's input.
application: The Supreme Court found that the Special Judge had acted improperly.
The Judge failed to follow the correct procedure by not first asking for the prosecution's opinion on the clerk's application.
Furthermore, the Judge made no effort to find out what evidence the clerk intended to disclose before granting the pardon.
The Court stated that the practice of a judge tendering a pardon 'suo motu' at the request of an accused is to be avoided.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the Special Judge had not exercised his discretion judicially or properly. However, the Court chose not to interfere with the order and dismissed the appeal. The reason for this was that the prosecution had subsequently stated in the High Court that it supported the decision to grant the pardon. Since the prosecution ultimately wanted the pardon to be tendered, the Court allowed it to stand despite the procedural errors made by the Special Judge.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the powers of the Special Judge in tendering pardon under s. 8(2) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act are limited to an application by the prosecution, or if the Judge can act suo motu.
appellant_arguments: The powers of the Special Judge in tendering pardon under s. 8(2) are limited to an application by the prosecution.
The Special Judge cannot act suo motu without being invited by the prosecution to consider the tender of pardon.
The granting of pardon to secure evidence is essentially for the prosecution to consider in the first instance.
respondent_arguments: The powers of the Special Judge to grant pardon are untrammelled and are not conditioned by the considerations the appellant relies on.
There is nothing in the section to show that the Special Judge must be moved by the prosecution.
The Judge may consider an offer by an accused, and such action is not outside his jurisdiction.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the powers of the Special Judge under s. 8(2) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act are circumscribed by the considerations that underlie s. 540 Cr. P. C., such that he could not acquit one accused so as to be able to convict another.
appellant_arguments: The powers of the Special Judge are circumscribed by considerations that underlie s. 540 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
The Judge can only act in the interests of justice and not with a view to granting an acquittal to one accused so as to be able to convict another.
No procedure or action can be in the interest of justice if it is prejudicial to an accused.
respondent_arguments: The powers of the Special Judge to grant pardon are untrammelled.
The sections in both the Code of Criminal Procedure and the Criminal Law Amendment Act related to tendering pardon are not conditioned by the considerations underlying s. 540 Cr. P. C.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Special Judge had exercised his discretion judicially and properly in tendering the pardon.
appellant_arguments: The Special Judge did not exercise his discretion judicially or properly.

Before tendering pardon, the Judge must know the nature of the evidence the person is likely to give, their complicity, and their degree of culpability, which the Judge made no effort to find out in this case.
The grant of pardon would be highly prejudicial to the defence of the other accused.
respondent_arguments: The discretion was properly exercised because the person pardoned (Jagasia) is an insignificant person compared with the main accused (contractors and superior officers).
The main accused are primarily responsible for defrauding the Government.

statutes.section: 8(3) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1952

cases.principle: The text only states this case was 'referred to' but does not specify the legal principle for which the Supreme Court relied on it. The court's reasoning is not shown to be based on this case.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Although the statutory power of a Special Judge to tender a pardon is wide and can be initiated upon an application by an accused, this power must be exercised on behalf of the prosecuting agency and only when the prosecution joins in the request. A Special Judge must not independently determine the propriety of tendering a pardon but must first refer the accused's request to the prosecution for its opinion.
obiter: Ordinarily, it is for the prosecution to ask that a particular accused be tendered a pardon.
The prosecution may not want to tender a pardon to the principal offender or the worst offender.
If the prosecution believes the tender of pardon is in the interest of a successful prosecution, it will likely agree.
The practice of a judge tendering a pardon suo motu at the request of an accused is to be avoided.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: While a Special Judge should not tender a pardon 'suo motu' at the request of an accused without first consulting the prosecution, the Judge's power to do so is not entirely barred. The proper procedure is for the Judge to refer the accused's request to the prosecuting agency for its opinion. In this case, although the Special Judge acted improperly by not following this procedure, the appeal was dismissed because the prosecution subsequently stated its agreement with the tender of pardon, thereby curing the initial procedural defect.
legal_tests_applied: To determine if a pardon is appropriate, a Judge must have material to assess the likely nature of the approver's testimony. Specifically, "Before the Special Judge acts to tender pardon, he must. of course, know the nature of the evidence the person seeking conditional pardon is likely to give, the nature of his complicity and the degree of his culpability in relation to the offence and in relation to the co-ac-cused."

When an accused directly applies for a pardon, the proper procedure is for the Judge to "first refer the reqquest to the prosecuting agency" and "ask for a statement from the prosecution on the request of the prisoner."
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument that the power to pardon under s. 8(2) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act is governed by s. 540 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was rejected. The court held, "There is no merit in the contention that s. 540 of the Code of Criminal Procedure governs... s. 8(2) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act," because the power to summon witnesses is distinct from the power to tender a pardon.

Although the court agreed with the appellant that the Special Judge had acted improperly and failed to exercise his discretion judicially by not first ascertaining the nature of the evidence or consulting the prosecution, the appeal failed because this procedural error was cured. The court stated, "But since the Public Prosecutor, when appearing in the High Court, stated that the prosecution also considered favourably the tender of pardon to Jagasia we say no more... since the prosecution in this case also wants that the tender of pardon be made it is obvious that the appeal must fail."

The court rejected the absolute proposition that a Special Judge can only act on an application by the prosecution, instead establishing a procedural requirement for the Judge to consult the prosecution when an accused makes a direct request.
why_respondent_won: The court affirmed the respondent's position that the power to tender pardon is not circumscribed by the considerations underlying s. 540 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, stating the two powers are not to be confused.

The respondent ultimately succeeded because the prosecution's eventual support for the pardon rendered the Special Judge's initial procedural failures moot. The court's decision to dismiss the appeal was based entirely on the fact that "the prosecution also considered favourably the tender of pardoo to the applicant."
The court accepted that a Judge is not jurisdictionally barred from considering a pardon request made directly by an accused, as long as the prosecution is brought into the decision-making process.
policy_considerations: The interests of the accused are as important as those of the prosecution, and "no procedure or action can be in the interest of justice if it is prejudicial to an accused."

A Special Judge must not act as a "veritable director of prosecution." The power to pardon is exercised on behalf of the prosecuting agency, not the Judge's own behalf, and should only be used when the prosecution joins in the request.
The decision to seek an approver's testimony is primarily for the prosecution, which may not need the evidence or may object to pardoning a particular accused who might be "the worst offender."
The court explicitly cautioned against the practice of judges tendering pardons 'suo motu' at the request of an accused, stating, "This practice is to be avoided."
